analysis.one_liner: Taxes large investment firms that buy single-family homes and forces them to sell to ordinary buyers.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the bill has six cosponsors — all Democrats or independents — and no hearing, vote, or action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax investment firms that manage pooled investor money every time they buy a house, and charge them $5,000 a year for every home they hold above a shrinking cap. Firms with $50 million or more in assets would have to cut their single-family holdings to zero over nine years; smaller pooled-money firms could keep up to 50. The yearly charges only stop when homes are sold to people who own no other residence — not to companies or other landlords — and firms above the caps would also lose their mortgage-interest and depreciation tax breaks. Despite the name, the bill's "hedge fund taxpayer" definition covers real estate trusts and partnerships that own single-family rentals, not just hedge funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and first-time buyers competing in neighborhoods where investment firms pay cash and outbid individual buyers, and renters in markets where large corporate landlords own many single-family homes. Because the sell-off requirement only counts sales to people who own no other home, houses would have to go to would-be owner-occupants rather than to another company, putting more homes within reach of people who want to live in them.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax on every single-family home an investment firm buys, equal to the greater of 15% of the purchase price or $10,000, raising the cost of the cash purchases that outbid families.

Charges $5,000 a year for every home a firm owns above a limit that shrinks each year, reaching zero for firms with $50 million or more in assets after nine years — meaning large corporate owners of houses would have to sell them all off.

Only sales to individuals who own no other single-family residence count toward the sell-off requirement, so the homes are steered to people buying a place to live rather than to other companies or landlords.
Strips mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions from firms that owe the tax, removing tax breaks that make buying houses to rent out more profitable than a family buying a home to live in.

Counts duplexes, triplexes, and fourplexes as single-family residences and aggregates related companies as one owner, closing common loopholes investors use to keep buying small residential properties.

analysis.who_pays: Hedge funds, private equity firms, and real estate investment trusts with $50 million or more in assets that own single-family rentals: they would pay the new purchase tax and the per-home yearly tax, phase their holdings down to zero over nine years, and lose mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions. Mid-size pooled-money firms would keep at most 50 homes. The taxes apply only to tax years beginning after enactment, so nothing is owed unless the bill becomes law.

drawbacks.text: The bill builds no housing. Home prices are driven largely by a shortage of homes, and this bill adds none — it reshuffles who owns existing houses — so in markets where big investors own a small share, prices may barely move.

Forced sell-offs could tighten rental markets in the short run: the only sales that count toward the requirement are to people who own no other home, so houses leave the rental stock before many renters are in a position to buy them.
The reach is narrower than the rhetoric: individual and small landlords — who own most rentals — are not covered at all, and mid-size pooled-money firms can keep 50 homes permanently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is the strong version of the idea: it does not just tax corporate landlords, it requires them to sell to residents and removes the tax breaks that make renting out houses more profitable than owning them. But an honest supporter has to admit the limits — the bill builds nothing, so it treats one cause of unaffordable housing without touching the bigger one (underbuilding), the forced sales could pinch renters before they help buyers, and most landlords are untouched because they are individuals or small firms rather than pooled-money investors. It is a targeted blow at a real and growing practice, not a fix for housing costs overall.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on Feb. 27, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee that same day.
The action record shows no hearing, markup, vote, or floor action of any kind since the referral.
Six senators have signed on as cosponsors — four Democrats and two independents — and no Republican has.
The bill's taxes would apply only to tax years beginning after enactment, so no firm owes anything and nothing in the housing market has changed yet.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the investment firms the bill targets — hedge funds, private equity, and real estate trusts that own single-family rentals — are better off: they face no new purchase tax, no per-home holding tax, and keep their mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions, so they can keep buying houses in competition with families.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HOPE for Homeownership Act on Feb. 27, 2025, taxing investment firms' single-family home purchases and requiring phased sell-offs to resident buyers; the bill was referred to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Six Senate cosponsors (Sens. King, Sanders, Van Hollen, Gallego, Kelly, and one additional Democrat)
for.role: Cosponsors, all from the Democratic caucus
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors — four Democrats and two independents; no Republican has joined.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: The bill sits in the committee he chairs; since its referral on Feb. 27, 2025, no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Corporate single-family rental industry (e.g., Invitation Homes, American Homes 4 Rent and their trade groups)
against.what_they_did: These firms are the bill's targets and would owe the new taxes; the industry actively lobbies Congress and state legislatures against limits on corporate homebuying.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors — Merkley and six cosponsors — are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee has not acted; no vote has occurred, so member-by-member positions are untested.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private equity firms with $50M+ in assets owning single-family rentals
industries.note: They would owe a tax on every home they buy (greater of 15% of price or $10,000), $5,000 a year per home above a limit phasing to zero over nine years, and would lose mortgage-interest and depreciation deductions. Their homes could only come off the books by selling to people who own no other residence. Their business model profits from owning houses that families would otherwise buy, so their interest runs against homebuyers here.

industries.industry: Single-family rental REITs and other pooled-money investment firms
industries.note: Real estate trusts and partnerships that manage investor money are covered even though they are not hedge funds in the everyday sense: those over $50 million in assets must sell everything, and smaller ones are capped at 50 homes. They profit from renting out houses at rents set in tight markets, which the bill's per-home tax is designed to reverse.

The bill explicitly exempts companies primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating single-family homes for sale, so new construction is untouched. If investors must sell to residents, more houses go to ordinary buyers, which feeds demand for for-sale builders rather than corporate landlords.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Finance Committee rarely reach the floor without a hearing, and tax bills almost always move as parts of larger packages. With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action since referral, the likeliest outcome is that the bill dies quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027, though versions of it could reappear in a future tax or housing package.
